Let $d,N,p\ge1$, $T>0$, $h=T/N$, and $t_n=nh$. Let $y:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ solve an initial-value problem in an open time-state domain $D$. Use the Euclidean norm $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], whose triangle inequality is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]. Let $\mathcal T\subset D$ be a common compact time-state tube with positive margin in $D$, and write $\mathcal T_t:=\{v\in\mathbb R^d:(t,v)\in\mathcal T\}$. Suppose a one-step map $\Psi_{h,n}$ is defined on $\mathcal T_{t_n}$, produces $y_{n+1}=\Psi_{h,n}(y_n)$, and the entire exact path, all numerical grid states, and every method stage lie in $\mathcal T$. If constants $C,C_0,L\ge0$, independent of $N$ and $n$, satisfy
$$\|y_0-y(0)\|_2\le C_0h^p,\qquad \|\Psi_{h,n}(y(t_n))-y(t_{n+1})\|_2\le Ch^{p+1},$$
and
$$\|\Psi_{h,n}(u)-\Psi_{h,n}(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$
for every $u,v\in\mathcal T_{t_n}$ and $0\le n<N$, then, for $L>0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le\left(C_0\exp(LT)+C\frac{\exp(LT)-1}{L}\right)h^p,$$
and, for $L=0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le(C_0+CT)h^p.$$

The chain rule and the derivative bound for $\Psi_n$ bound the derivative of its composition with this segment by $(1+Lh)\|x_n-u_n\|$; the vector mean value inequality [F1] therefore gives its endpoint Lipschitz bound with constant $1+Lh$. For $d=0$, the state difference and both endpoint values lie in the zero vector space, so the same bound is immediate. Consequently $$e_{n+1}\le(1+Lh)e_n+c_vh^{p+1}.$$ By [F3], $e_n\le Xh^p$.

The exact tangent and adjoint recurrences give $$\|S_{n+1}\|\le(1+Lh)\|S_n\|+Mh,\qquad \|p(t_n)\|\le(1+Lh)\|p(t_{n+1})\|+Mh.$$ Expanding these finite recurrences and using $(1+Lh)^k\le e^{LT}$ shows $\|S_n\|\le\overline S$ and $\|p(t_n)\|\le\overline P$. These bounds include $L=0$. For any one of the four derivative maps, comparison at numerical and exact nodes gives $$\|F_n^h(x_n,\theta)-F_n^e(u_n,\theta)\|\le c_1h^{p+1}+Hh e_n\le Rh^{p+1}.$$

The actual differentiated numerical graph satisfies $S_{n+1}^h=A_n^h(x_n)S_n^h+B_n^h(x_n)$. Subtract the exact recurrence and split the matrix product using $A_n^h(S_n^h-S_n)+(A_n^h-A_n^e)S_n$. Hence $$\|S_{n+1}^h-S_{n+1}\|\le(1+Lh)\|S_n^h-S_n\|+R(\overline S+1)h^{p+1}.$$ The initial derivative bound and [F3] yield $C_Sh^p$.

At the terminal node, the difference of adjoint seeds is at most $Dh^p$. Subtract the two backward recurrences, splitting $A_h^Tp_h-A_e^Tp_e=A_h^T(p_h-p_e)+(A_h-A_e)^Tp_e$. The Euclidean operator norm of a transpose equals that of the matrix. For every finite-dimensional Euclidean vector $v$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|v\|=\sup_{\|w\|\le1}|w^Tv|$: if $v\ne0$, equality is attained at $w=v/\|v\|$, while for $v=0$ both sides vanish, including in dimension zero. Applying this closed-unit-ball formula to both sides of the pairing gives the transpose identity in all finite dimensions. Therefore $$\|p_n^h-p(t_n)\|\le(1+Lh)\|p_{n+1}^h-p(t_{n+1})\|+R(\overline P+1)h^{p+1}.$$ Reverse the indices and apply [F3]. This gives $C_Ph^p$.

receipt_excerpt.quote:
Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:D\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$
([[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]), let $x\in D$, and let
$p\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$. Define the open parameter set $S_{x,p}:=\{t\in\mathbb R:x+tp\in D\}$,
which contains $0$, the feasible ray $T_{x,p}:=S_{x,p}\cap[0,\infty)$,
and $\phi(t):=f(x+tp)$ for $t\in S_{x,p}$. At every $t\in S_{x,p}$,
including $0$, the chain rule gives $\phi'(t)=Df(x+tp)p$.
By [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],
the matrix of $Df$ is the Jacobian, whose scalar-field row is the transpose
of the gradient. Hence
$\phi'(t)=\langle\nabla f(x+tp),p\rangle$, using the gradient convention
of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the Euclidean inner product of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. A direction is a **descent direction** at
$x$ when $\phi'(0)=\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle<0$.

Assume for the line-search conditions below that $p$ is a descent direction
at $x$.
Fix constants $0<c_1<c_2<1/2$. A feasible step $t>0$ is a **Wolfe step**
when
$$
\phi(t)\le\phi(0)+c_1t\phi'(0),\qquad \phi'(t)\ge c_2\phi'(0).
$$
It is a **strong Wolfe step** when it satisfies the first inequality and
$$
|\phi'(t)|\le c_2|\phi'(0)|.
$$
The first inequality is the Armijo sufficient-decrease condition. The second
Wolfe inequality is the curvature condition. Every strong Wolfe step is a
Wolfe step, because $\phi'(0)<0$ and the strong curvature bound implies
$\phi'(t)\ge-c_2|\phi'(0)|=c_2\phi'(0)$.

For a descent direction define its **descent angle** $\theta\in[0,\pi/2)$ by
$$
\cos\theta:=-\frac{\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle}{\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\|p\|_2}.
$$
The denominator is nonzero for a descent direction. The Cauchy–Schwarz
inequality [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]] ensures $0<\cos\theta\le1$.

Use the operationwise real/complex arithmetic model, with six-real-operation complex products and componentwise division by positive real scalars. A scaled norm of a nonzero complex vector first chooses the largest absolute real or imaginary component $s>0$, rounds every real component divided by $s$, sums their rounded squares sequentially, rounds the positive square root, and rounds multiplication by $s$. A norm of already scaled components omits the last multiplication. Zero input has exact norm zero. Reject every nonzero exact intermediate outside the normal range, nonfinite/invalid operation, and nonpositive required norm; return the first range-failure. All sign changes and conjugations are exact.

For a Householder active block $C=[x\;B]$, $x\in\mathbb C^r$, a zero $x$ copies the block with identity action. Otherwise compute $\widehat N$ by the scaled norm.
